proof:
Let $\nu_\ell$ sum the full $m$-volumes of $Q_{\ell,j}$ at their coarse bases. Write $J=|P|$. The cell estimate in the proof of e4ef1ac154c5d280 applies to each coarse fiber and to its trace in every closed ambient halfspace. The error between $\mu_\ell$ and $\nu_\ell$ for these halfspaces and for total mass is bounded by $J\,2r\delta_\ell(2R+2\delta_\ell)^{m-1}\to0$. The estimate counts sampled mass on any prelimit null coarse fiber.

Hausdorff convergence of compact convex sets gives uniform convergence of their support functions. If $Q_j$ has positive volume, every interior point has a small ball contained in all sufficiently late $Q_{\ell,j}$ by this convergence and separation, and every exterior point is eventually outside. Since the boundary is null, the indicators converge in $L^1$ in the common box. If $Q_j$ has zero volume, the late sets lie in shrinking neighborhoods of the compact null set $Q_j$ and their volume tends to zero, giving the same $L^1$ conclusion. Thus $\nu_\ell\to\nu_*$ in unnormalized total variation. Adding the cell error gives uniform unnormalized fine-to-limit halfspace discrepancy and convergence of fine totals to $M_*$. The positivity of $M_*$ then gives uniform normalized closed-halfspace discrepancy by subtracting the two ratios. The normalized depths at every same ambient mark differ by at most this discrepancy because they are infima over the same containing cuts.

Depth for $\nu_*/M_*$ is Lipschitz in the last $m$ coordinates at any fixed coarse base. One can take the infimum over through-mark halfspaces by translating each containing cut parallel toward the mark. If the continuous part of the normal is zero, the cut does not change when the mark is moved at its fixed coarse base. Otherwise normalize that part to unit length. Every fiber threshold moves by at most the displacement norm, independently of the coarse coefficients, and a slab of width $t$ has volume at most $t(2R\sqrt m)^{m-1}$ per fiber by orthogonal Fubini in the containing ball of radius $R\sqrt m$, with section bound one at $m=1$. Sum over $P$, divide by $M_*$, and take infima. This proves continuity even at a base whose own fiber has zero volume, and the compact finite union $S_*$ admits a maximizing mark. An interior ball in any positive-volume fiber gives positive depth at its center, since any closed cut containing that center retains at least half the ball in the fiber.

The original sets give $P=\operatorname{conv}(P)\cap\mathbb Z^k$, since a convex combination of points from nonempty coarse fibers is feasible in each $C_\ell$. For any integer $j=\sum_i\lambda_i j_i$ with $j_i\in P$, pass to the limit in the anchored Minkowski inclusion to get $\sum_i\lambda_iQ_{j_i}\subset Q_j$. Indeed approximate each chosen point in $Q_{j_i}$ by one in $Q_{\ell,j_i}$ and pass to its weighted limit at $j$. Hence $D=\operatorname{conv}S_*$ has exactly the given integer coarse fibers. A positive-depth mark has coarse base in the hull of the positive-volume bases, since otherwise a purely coarse closed halfspace through it strictly separates it from those bases and has mass zero. The limiting inclusion puts a positively scaled translate of a full-dimensional source fiber into the own fiber of such a mark.

For the limsup, select approximate maximizing fine marks along a subsequence realizing that limsup. Compact bounds and finiteness of $P$ give a further subsequence with one coarse base and a continuous-coordinate limit in $Q_j$. The fixed-base continuity and same-point uniform discrepancy bound the limsup by the limiting maximum. For the liminf take a positive-depth limiting mark, move it slightly into its full-dimensional own fiber, and fix that interior mark. A ball about it is in every sufficiently late $Q_{\ell,j}$. The cubes of radius $\delta_\ell$ in maximum norm centered at the actual sample coset cover all fine coordinates. They cover almost everywhere by the cell tiling and their locally finite union is closed. Replace only the first $r$ fiber coordinates by a point of this coset at Euclidean distance at most $\sqrt r\,\delta_\ell$. This is feasible in the late fibers. The fixed-base Lipschitz bound and the uniform normalized discrepancy recover the depth at the interior mark in the limit. Let the interior perturbation tend to zero and take a maximizing limiting mark. The two inequalities prove convergence.

To realize the exact limiting trace in a full-dimensional body, if $\operatorname{aff}(P)=\mathbb R^k$ then $D$ already has full dimension because one fiber has positive $m$-volume and its projection spans the coarse space. Otherwise $\operatorname{conv}(P)$ is at positive distance from $\mathbb Z^k\setminus P$ by compactness and completeness. Choose a convex open neighborhood of $\operatorname{conv}(P)$ within this distance. Take a small closed ambient ball with its base projection in the neighborhood and strictly on one side of a hyperplane containing $\operatorname{aff}(P)$. Its hull with $D$ is full dimensional, projects within the neighborhood, and adds no new integer base. A convex combination over any base in $P$ cannot use positive weight from the ball by applying the separating affine functional, which vanishes on $\operatorname{aff}(P)$. All original fibers therefore remain unchanged.

For fixed $C$ the convergence is the asserted fixed-body limit. The constant comparison $2^r\Gamma_m>\Gamma_s$ follows from $\Gamma_m>1/e>1/4$ and $\Gamma_s\le1/2$ for $s\ge1$, or from $2^{-r}\le1/4$ for $s=0,r\ge2$. At $r=1,s=0$ the constants coincide and the limit gives no strict margin. A strict gap yields actual sufficiently late marks above the fine threshold. When $k=0$, apply the full-mass case of 6769574fc1bd9f8d to the positive-volume fixed $m$-body. The separate one-dimensional counting case with $k=0,r=1,s=0$ follows by taking a median of the nonempty sampled progression.

statement:
Let $k\ge0$, $r\ge1$, $s\ge0$, and $m=r+s$. Let $C_\ell\subset\mathbb R^k\times\mathbb R^r\times\mathbb R^s$ be compact and convex, with the same finite set $P\subset\mathbb Z^k$ of all nonempty coarse integer fibers. Suppose these fibers $Q_{\ell,j}\subset[-R,R]^m$ converge individually in Hausdorff distance to nonempty $Q_j$, and $M_*=\sum_{j\in P}|Q_j|_m>0$. Sample the first $r$ fiber coordinates on any full-rank cosets $a_\ell+L_\ell$, with measurable fundamental cells of $L_\ell$ contained in $[-\delta_\ell,\delta_\ell]^r$ and $\delta_\ell\to0$. Let $\mu_\ell$ be the sum of $s$-volumes at the sampled pairs $(j,\lambda)$, multiplied by the covolume of $L_\ell$, using counting for $s=0$. Put $S_*=\bigcup_{j\in P}(\{j\}\times Q_j)$ and let $\nu_*$ sum the full $m$-volumes on these fibers. All depths are normalized and use closed ambient halfspaces.

The fine mass is eventually positive. The supremum of fine depth over the actual sampled trace of $C_\ell$ converges to the maximum $\nu_*$ depth over $S_*$. Each positive-depth limiting mark can be recovered to arbitrary depth accuracy by fine marks at the same coarse base. There is a full-dimensional compact convex body with exactly the lifted fibers $S_*$ at all integer coarse bases, including the nonempty fibers of zero $m$-volume.

In particular this gives the fixed-body limit for $C_\ell=C$ and positive coarse mass. In that fixed-body setting, write $\Gamma_j=(j/(j+1))^j$ for $j\ge1$ and $\Gamma_0=1$. If the coarse depth is at least $2^{-k}\Gamma_m$, then sufficiently late fine traces have a point of depth at least $2^{-k-r}\Gamma_s$ in the strict cases $(r,s)\ne(1,0)$. The coarse premise holds for $k=0$ by ordinary centroid depth.
title: Exact fine-lattice depth limit with converging coarse fibers
